metadata.title: Build MCPB
metadata.subtitle: Packaged, Not Sandboxed
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does bundling a local MCP server as an MCPB make it sandboxed or otherwise safer to run? Lands the carry-out that packaging buys runnability without a toolchain, not safety - the env var name still has to match exactly and every path check is still the developer's to write.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Here's what's actually happening: packaging a server as an MCPB doesn't make it safe to run — it makes it runnable without your dev toolchain installed. Safety is still entirely on you.

beats.narration_text: Hear "package my server as an MCPB" and the word 'package' pulls you toward 'container' — as if bundling itself hardens the code. That reading is the trap.

Open the manifest. Look for a permissions block, a sandbox field, an allowed-paths list — there is none. The packaged MCPB runs with exactly the file access the unpackaged script had. Package a path bug in, and it still walks straight out of its own folder.

shot.new_visual_element: SAME ACCESS AS THE RAW SCRIPT

production_viz.label: SAME ACCESS AS THE RAW SCRIPT

production_viz.caption: packaging changed nothing it can touch

beats.narration_text: Here's the anchor. Your manifest launches the server with one setting: an environment variable named ROOT_DIR, pointing at the folder the user picked at install time. Hold onto that name.

Here's what an MCPB actually is: a zip file. Inside it, manifest.json, a server folder with your code and dependencies, an icon. The host reads the manifest and launches mcp_config's command exactly as written — dollar-dirname substitutes bundle-relative paths, dollar-user-config substitutes install-time values like the folder the user picked.

They optimized for exactness over ergonomics. The env var name is whatever you wrote in the manifest — no auto-prefix, no case transform. Write ROOT_DIR in the manifest but read ROOT_DIRECTORY in your server code, and the value comes back empty. No error, no crash — the config is quietly dropped on the floor.

So back to ROOT_DIR. Get the name right, and that path flows straight into your handler unchecked — the host doesn't validate it, doesn't bound it, doesn't touch it. Because there's no sandbox, one unvalidated dot-dot-slash in a filename walks the server right out of its own folder.

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — NO CHECK ON IT
production_viz.caption: right name, still no sandbox

beats.narration_text: Neither symptom proves what you'd want it to. A packaged MCPB that runs fine on your machine doesn't prove it's safe anywhere else — your dev toolchain may have quietly filled a gap. An MCPB that fails on a clean machine doesn't mean the packaging step is broken — usually one dependency never got bundled in.
Here's what packaging bought you: runnability without a toolchain. Here's what it didn't buy you: safety. The env var name still has to match exactly, and every path check is still yours to write.

props.quote: Packaging a server as an MCPB makes it runnable without a toolchain — it doesn't make it safe. The env var name still has to match exactly, and every path check is still yours to write.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Ask it to walk the MCPB mechanism, then build a threat model against a real example: an MCPB that reads files from a directory the user picks at install time. Make it show its work on three checks — env var name match, path validation, and whether the build script actually bundles the dependencies. Go deeper: ask it to compare MCPB packaging to real sandboxing — WASM, seccomp, a container runtime — and design what a truly bounded MCP server would look like.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm building an MCP server and considering packaging it as an MCPB (Anthropic's bundle format for MCP servers). Walk me through the mechanism first: what's inside an MCPB, how the host launches it via mcp_config, and what user_config plus its environment variables (e.g. ROOT_DIR) actually do at install time. Then help me build a threat model against a concrete example — an MCPB that reads files from a directory the user picks at install time. Cover three checks specifically: (1) does the env var name in the manifest's mcp_config exactly match what my server code reads (name-match trap — 'ROOT_DIR' in the manifest vs. 'ROOT_DIRECTORY' in code fails silently), (2) does my server validate that every requested path stays inside the configured root, or would a dot-dot-slash escape it (unvalidated-path trap — nothing outside your code bounds this), (3) does my build script bundle dependencies with esbuild, or does it assume node_modules will be present on the target machine (missing-bundle trap). For each check, give me the specific code to add or verify, name what would still be missing at the end, and be honest about what packaging does not do.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: compare MCPB packaging to real sandboxing primitives — WASM, seccomp, or a container runtime — and design what a truly bounded MCP server would look like. Where would the boundary live, who would enforce it, and what would that cost in developer ergonomics?
